content: The combination of sofosbuvir and velpatasvir (SOF-VEL) demonstrates slightly higher efficacy compared to the combination of sofosbuvir, ledipasvir, and daclatasvir (SOF-LDV/DCL), as evidenced by available data. However, SOF-VEL remains more expensive in many settings. Based on data from India, under specific assumptions, SOF-VEL appears to be cost-effective when compared to SOF-LDV/DCL. The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) is approximately $900–$1000 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained for patients without cirrhosis and $1700–$1850 per QALY gained for those with cirrhosis. For SOF-VEL to achieve cost neutrality compared to SOF-LDV/DCL, its price would need to be reduced to below $145 for a 4-week treatment course, according to unpublished data from India (personal communication with Rakesh Aggarwal). Regarding the combination of glecaprevir and pibrentasvir (G/P), the originating company has not yet finalized its access strategy. The World Health Organization (WHO) has been informed that the company is exploring several access options. Currently, this combination is registered only in the USA and a few high-income countries. The price for an 8-week treatment course in the USA is $26,000. The first oral direct-acting antiviral (DAA) was approved in 2013, and over one million patients with hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection have been successfully treated worldwide. However, with the exception of Egypt, most DAA treatments have been provided in high-income countries, as noted in the WHO Global Report on Access to Hepatitis C Treatment (October 2016). The use of pangenotypic DAA regimens could eliminate several barriers to rapid treatment scale-up, such as the need for genotyping prior to treatment initiation, and simplify treatment decision-making. The recommendations outlined in this document are particularly relevant for lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) with access to generic DAAs. Currently, over 110 countries have access to at least one generic DAA. As treatment programs expand, ensuring the quality of the drug supply is critical. As of September 2017, the WHO prequalification program has approved daclatasvir from the innovator company and generic sofosbuvir produced by the Indian company Mylan. Other generic DAAs on the market have not yet been approved by stringent regulatory authorities or prequalified by WHO, but this is expected to change as several products are advancing in the prequalification process. This will facilitate the procurement of generic treatments by both international and domestic programs. The availability of WHO-prequalified generic DAAs has increased between mid-2015 and September 2017. Prices for generic DAAs have continued to decline during this period, although the prices for the generic pangenotypic SOF-VEL regimen remain somewhat higher than those for older DAA combinations. It is anticipated that these prices will decrease further as the market matures. The WHO recommends the use of pangenotypic DAA regimens for the treatment of individuals aged 18 years and older with chronic HCV infection. The rationale for this recommendation includes the following points: The clinical benefits of pangenotypic regimens are comparable to those of non-pangenotypic regimens. Pangenotypic regimens eliminate the need for genotyping, which is a costly process. They simplify medicine procurement and supply chains. They offer a simplified treatment scheme, which can reduce the risk of patients being lost to follow-up. Countries should plan for a transition to the use of pangenotypic regimens. The speed of this transition will depend on the prevalence of HCV infection, the distribution of HCV genotypes, and the effectiveness of current regimens in treating these genotypes. Research gaps remain, including the need for data on the efficacy and safety of pangenotypic regimens in specific populations, such as those with severe renal impairment, individuals under 18 years of age, and pregnant women. Additionally, predictive factors for selecting patients who could benefit from shorter treatment durations need to be investigated. Cost-effectiveness data for pangenotypic regimens in LMICs and the clinical significance of drug resistance also require further study. Data on treatment failure and its relationship with rare genotypes and resistance are also needed.
